fields.h1: The God of All Comfort by Hannah Whitall Smith: A Study Guide
fields.meta_title: The God of All Comfort by Hannah Whitall Smith — Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A warm, answer-first study guide to Hannah Whitall Smith’s The God of All Comfort — its aim, structure, central themes of God’s trustworthiness and the rest of faith, who should read it, and reflection questions. Read the full text free on Ochorus.
fields.body_html:
If your faith has ever felt like a weight you carry rather than a rest you lean into, Hannah Whitall Smith wrote The God of All Comfort for you. Published in 1906, near the end of a long and much-tested life, it is her warm, unhurried answer to one question: what is God actually like? Her conviction is that most of our spiritual distress comes not from our sins or our circumstances but from a low, fearful, mistaken picture of the One we are trusting. Change that picture, she argues, and the anxious, up-and-down Christian life gives way to a settled peace. This guide summarises the book, walks through how it is built, and offers ways to read it slowly for yourself. You can read the full text free here on Ochorus, in The God of All Comfort.

What the book is, and what it is for

The title comes straight from Scripture — the God of all comfort is Paul’s phrase in 2 Corinthians 1:3 — and the whole book is an extended meditation on taking that name seriously. Smith had spent decades in the holiness and higher-life movements, and she had watched sincere believers make themselves miserable: forever examining their feelings, forever anxious about their coldness, forever afraid they did not truly belong to God. Her aim is plainly stated and pastoral. She wants to dispel the doubt and gloom that shadow so many devout people, and to replace them with the quiet confidence of a child who simply believes what a good Father has said.

She is careful, at the outset, to say what the book is not. It does not argue about the authenticity of the Bible or wrestle with theological controversy; others, she says, are far more capable of that. It is written instead for ordinary believers who already accept Christ and want to know how His comfort can become their daily experience. The problem she diagnoses is not unbelief in the intellectual sense but a failure to receive. God is continually offering comfort, she insists, yet it never reaches a heart that will not take Him at His word:

“What greater comfort could there be than this—that the Creator of Heaven and earth takes responsibility for our care?”

Hannah Whitall Smith

How the book is structured

The God of All Comfort is a set of seventeen short chapters, each one turning over a single facet of God’s character or a single obstacle to resting in it. There is no rigid system; the chapters read like a series of settling, reassuring conversations, and any one of them can stand alone.

The opening chapter, “Why This Book Has Been Written,” sets the diagnosis and the cure. From there Smith moves through the names and nature of God — “What is His Name?”, the title chapter “The God of All Comfort,” “The Lord Our Shepherd,” “He Spoke to Them of the Father,” “Jehovah,” “The Lord is Good,” and “The Lord Our Dwelling Place.” Each one presses a single truth: that the God we actually have is better than the anxious God we imagine.

The later chapters turn from God’s character to our response. “Much More Versus Much Less,” “Self-Examination,” and “Things That Cannot Be Shaken” deal with how we look at ourselves; “A Word to the Wavering Ones,” “Discouragement,” “The Shout of Faith,” and “Thanksgiving Versus Complaining” address the moods and habits that rob us of rest. The book climbs to two summits: “Conformed to the Image of Christ,” and the closing chapter, “God is Enough,” which gathers everything into one ringing conclusion.

The central themes

The trustworthiness of God. Everything in the book rests here. Smith returns again and again to the idea that God is not the stern, reluctant judge our fears invent but a tender, actively caring parent. She loves the mother-image the prophets use — as one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you (Isaiah 66:13) — and she leans on the promise I will comfort you; be not afraid in the spirit of Isaiah 41:10. When Israel complained that the Lord had forgotten them, His answer, she notes, was the tenderest of questions: can a mother forget her child (Isaiah 49:15)? To know God like this is to have the ground of all comfort.

The rest of faith. Comfort, for Smith, is not a feeling we manufacture but a truth we accept. She uses homely pictures — a passenger cannot relax until she believes the conductor that she is on the right train, a traveler cannot feel safe until he trusts the guide — to show that belief comes first and feeling follows. This is why she can say so bluntly that being at rest is an act of the will, not a mood that happens to us:

“Being comforted is not passive; it involves the will. We must choose it.”

Hannah Whitall Smith

The same conviction shapes her counsel about promises like Christ’s let not your hearts be troubled (John 14:27), the angel’s good news of great joy for all people (Luke 2:10), and the Lord’s reminder to consider the birds of the air (Matthew 6:26). These are not merely to be admired; they are to be believed, and then the anxiety lifts. Her remedy is startlingly practical: cast your care on Him because He cares for you (1 Peter 5:7), and refuse the voices of doubt.

“If we desire comfort, we must choose to believe every word of comfort God has spoken.”

Hannah Whitall Smith

Guidance and the shepherding God. In “The Lord Our Shepherd” and “The Lord Our Dwelling Place” Smith takes up two of the great resting-places of the Psalms — the shepherd who leads and provides (Psalm 23:1) and the God who has been our dwelling place in all generations (Psalm 90:1). Her point is that guidance is not an anxious hunt for a hidden will but the natural care of a shepherd for sheep who simply follow. We are not asked to find the way; we are asked to trust the One who does.

Doubt and discouragement. The chapter “Discouragement” is one of the book’s most bracing. Smith flatly denies that low spirits are a form of humility or piety. Discouragement, she says, dries up faith at the root, because according to your faith be it done to you (Matthew 9:29) — and where discouragement rules, it is done to us according to our discouragement instead.

“Since faith and discouragement cannot exist together, discouragement is an absolute barrier to faith.”

Hannah Whitall Smith

Her cure is memorably plain: do not argue with discouragement, simply give it up. She points to the Lord’s own charter for good cheer — take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33) — and to David, who, with his city burned and his men ready to stone him, strengthened himself in the Lord his God (1 Samuel 30:6). Set against this steadiness is her final, joyful summit, built on the psalmist’s for God alone, O my soul, wait in silence (Psalm 62:5-7):

“The last and greatest lesson that the soul has to learn is the fact that God, and God alone, is enough for all its needs. This is the lesson that all His dealings with us are meant to teach; and this is the crowning discovery of our whole Christian life. GOD IS ENOUGH!”

Hannah Whitall Smith

Who should read it

This is a book for the weary believer more than the curious inquirer. If you are a Christian who loves God but cannot seem to enjoy Him — who prays and reads and serves yet lives on a spiritual rollercoaster of highs and crashes — Smith is writing directly to you. She is also a wise companion for anyone battling chronic discouragement, anxiety, or the nagging fear that they are not good enough for grace. Her answer to that last fear is characteristically freeing:

“Christ came to save sinners, not those who think themselves worthy. Your need is your qualification.”

Hannah Whitall Smith

Readers who love the classic devotional voice — Andrew Murray, Amy Carmichael, the Puritans at their warmest — will feel at home here. And because Smith writes with such plainness and such motherly kindness, the book suits new believers and seasoned ones alike. It is short enough to read in a few sittings and rich enough to return to for years.

How to read it today

Read it slowly, and one chapter at a time. Because each chapter circles a single truth about God, the book rewards being taken as a daily reading rather than devoured at a sitting — one theme to carry through the day and test against your own worries.

Keep a Bible open beside it. Smith is saturated in Scripture, and much of the book’s power comes from letting her quoted verses do their work; look up the passages she leans on — Isaiah 41:10, John 14:27, Psalm 62:5-7 — and read them in their setting. It also helps to read against the grain of your own instincts: when Smith says comfort is a choice, notice the places where you have been waiting for a feeling instead. Try turning a chapter into a small experiment for the day, deliberately believing one promise you have only ever admired.

Finally, read it alongside her other work. The God of All Comfort is the mature companion to her most famous book; where that one teaches the how of a surrendered life, this one steadies the who of the God you are surrendering to. If it feeds you, go on to The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life and to her spiritual autobiography, The Unselfishness of God, and explore more of her writing on her author page, Hannah Whitall Smith. Everything loss, as Paul says, compared to knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8) — and knowing Him truly is exactly what Smith is after.

For reflection

These questions are for personal journaling or a small group. Let them slow you down.

  1. Smith argues that most of our distress comes from a mistaken picture of God. If you drew an honest portrait of the God you actually expect to meet in prayer, what would He look like — and how does 2 Corinthians 1:3 challenge it?
  2. She insists that comfort must be received, not merely offered. Where in your life are you waiting to feel comforted before you will believe God’s word to you?
  3. In the chapter on discouragement she calls low spirits a barrier to faith, not a form of humility. Is there a discouragement you have been quietly nursing as though it were pious? What would it mean to simply give it up?
  4. Which of God’s names in the book — Shepherd, Father, Dwelling Place, the God of all comfort — do you most need this season, and why?
  5. The book ends with three words: God is enough. What are you currently treating as though you needed it in addition to God, and how would Psalm 62:5-7 speak to that?

When you are ready, begin with the first chapter of The God of All Comfort and let Hannah Whitall Smith introduce you, slowly and kindly, to the God who is better than your fears.
